nameStory: The 'goldenbanner' name comes from the bright yellow, banner-like flowers that wave in clusters above the foliage like tiny golden flags. The 'spreadfruit' part refers to how the seed pods spread outward from the stem at wide angles when mature, creating a distinctive splayed appearance.
description: Spreadfruit goldenbanner is a bushy perennial wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with clusters of bright yellow, pea-like flowers. Like other members of the legume family, it has three-leaflet leaves and produces flattened seed pods. This western native is extremely rare in New England, with only a couple of documented sightings, making it a true botanical treasure if you're lucky enough to spot one.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers arranged in upright clusters, each flower about 3/4 inch long with the classic pea-flower shape - one large upper petal (banner), two side petals (wings), and a lower keel

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with three oval leaflets arranged like a clover, each leaflet 1-3 inches long with a smooth, slightly waxy feel and prominent veining

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened, hairy seed pods 2-3 inches long that spread outward from the stem at wide angles, turning brown and papery when mature with a rustling sound when touched

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy, upright perennial 1-3 feet tall with multiple stems arising from the base, forming loose colonies through underground rhizomes

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Green to reddish stems that feel somewhat ridged to the touch and are covered with fine, soft hairs that give them a slightly fuzzy texture

habitat: In its native western range, it prefers dry, sandy or rocky soils in open meadows and hillsides. The extremely rare New England occurrences have been in disturbed sites, possibly as escaped garden plants or accidental introductions. Look for it in sunny, well-drained locations with poor to moderate soil.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges in late spring with the distinctive three-leaflet leaves appearing first on reddish stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in early to mid-summer with showy golden-yellow flower clusters that are hard to miss. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and turn brown, splitting open to release seeds. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground rhizomes, leaving no above-ground parts visible.

funFact: This plant is basically a botanical tourist in New England - it's so far outside its natural western range that seeing one here is like spotting a cactus in Maine, making any New England sighting a genuine botanical mystery worth reporting to local naturalist groups.
confusionNotes: The three-leaflet leaves might remind you of clover, but the upright growth habit and showy yellow flower spikes are completely different from clover's round flower heads. Wild lupine has similar pea-flowers but grows much taller and has 7-11 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand.
contextualKnowledge: This is primarily a western North American species that somehow made its way to New England, possibly through gardening or seed contamination. Any sighting in New England is botanically significant and worth documenting, as it helps scientists track plant migrations and introductions.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Aaron's rod (Thermopsis villosa), spreadfruit goldenbanner is generally smaller and more compact, with seed pods that distinctly spread outward rather than pointing upward. Aaron's rod also has denser, more silvery hairs on its stems and leaves, giving it a more gray-green appearance overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Aaron's rod differs from its relative spreadfruit goldenbanner by having more densely hairy (villous) stems and leaves, giving it a distinctly fuzzy appearance.
